claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-type high-entropy alloy containing dual FCC and BCC lamellar phases.
The dual-phase lamellae are hierarchically organized into colonies.
The FCC/BCC phase boundaries are semi-coherent.
These phase boundaries hinder dislocation motion and produce high dislocation density and local stress concentration.
A single short post-casting annealing step at a moderately elevated temperature can beneficially modify the alloy.
Annealing can modify the semi-coherent boundaries through slight thermal disordering or an interfacial phase transformation.
The modified boundaries facilitate more uniform dislocation motion across the phases.
Annealing reduces abrupt mismatch and internal stress concentrations at phase boundaries.
Reducing dislocation accumulation and pile-ups delays crack initiation and propagation.
A controlled anneal preserves second-phase strengthening.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or increase its yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
More homogeneous plastic deformation is responsible for the predicted simultaneous retention or enhancement of strength and ductility.
The untreated alloy has high strength at room temperature.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
The untreated alloy's limited ductility and brittleness result from localized dislocation pile-ups near semi-coherent phase boundaries.
Excessive annealing-induced coarsening or unwanted phase transformation would compromise lamellar second-phase strengthening.
Thermomechanical processing of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 can produce heterogeneous microstructures and simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
